summary.text: Letting \(B=\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor+1\) and \(T=B^3\), take all integers up to \(T\) together with all primes up to \(n\); every \(k\le n\) factors inside this set, since either all its prime factors are at most \(B\) and can be split into two factors at most \(T\), or its largest prime factor exceeds \(B\) and its complementary factor is at most \(T\). Thus \(a(n)\le \pi(n)+O(n^{3/4})\), while the bounds \(4^m\le m\binom{2m}{m}\le m(2m)^{\pi(2m)}\), followed by logarithmic estimates, give \(m^{3/4}\le \pi(2m)\) eventually; this controls the ratio for large \(n\), and the remaining finite range is bounded trivially.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_n=\{1,2,\ldots,n\},
\qquad
S\cdot S=\{xy:x,y\in S\},
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the minimum cardinality of a set \(S\subseteq T_n\) such that \(T_n\subseteq S\cdot S\). We prove that there is an absolute constant \(C\) such that
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le C\qquad(n\ge2),
\]
where \(\pi(n)\) is the number of primes at most \(n\).

The proof begins with a factor-balancing lemma.

**Factor-balancing lemma.** Suppose \(B,T,N,m\) are nonnegative integers satisfying
\[
T>0,\qquad BN\le T^2,\qquad m\le N,
\]
and every prime divisor of \(m\) is at most \(B\). Then there are positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
m=xy,\qquad x\le T,\qquad y\le T.
\]

We prove this by strong induction on \(m\). If \(m\le T\), take \(x=1\) and \(y=m\). (The case \(m=0\) cannot arise in the later application; in the stated induction the displayed hypotheses together with the branch in which this choice is used give the needed bounds.) Now suppose \(m>T\). Since \(T>0\), we have \(m>1\), so some prime \(p\) divides \(m\). Write
\[
m=pq.
\]
Since \(p\ge2\) and \(q>0\), we have \(q<m\). Every prime divisor of \(q\) is also a prime divisor of \(m\), so it is at most \(B\); also \(q\le m\le N\). The induction hypothesis therefore gives
\[
q=xy,\qquad x,y\le T.
\]
If \(px\le T\), then \(m=(px)y\) is the required factorization. If \(py\le T\), then \(m=x(py)\) is the required factorization. If neither inequality holds, then
\[
T<px,\qquad T<py,
\]
so
\[
T^2<(px)(py)=p^2xy=pm.
\]
On the other hand, \(p\le B\) and \(m\le N\), whence \(pm\le BN\le T^2\), a contradiction. This proves the lemma.

We now construct a covering set. Let
\[
r=\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor,
\qquad B=r+1,
\qquad T=B^3.
\]
Here \(r\) means the integer fourth root, characterized by \(r^4\le n<(r+1)^4\). Define
\[
S_n=\{1,2,\ldots,\min(T,n)\}\ \cup\ \{p:p\text{ is prime and }p\le n\}.
\]
Plainly \(S_n\subseteq T_n\).

We record the numerical relations needed to apply the factor-balancing lemma. Since \(B=r+1\ge1\), we have \(T=B^3>0\). The defining property of the integer fourth root gives
\[
n<B^4.
\]
Thus \(n\le B^4\), and, since \(B\ge1\), also \(n\le B^5\). Consequently
\[
Bn\le B^6=T^2,
\qquad
n\le B^4=BT.
\tag{1}
\]

We claim that every \(k\in T_n\) is a product of two members of \(S_n\). First note that \(1\in S_n\). If \(k\) is prime, then both \(k\) and \(1\) belong to \(S_n\), and \(k=k\cdot1\). Similarly, if \(k\le T\), then \(k,1\in S_n\), so again \(k=k\cdot1\).

It remains to consider \(k>T\) which is not prime. Let \(P\) be the largest prime divisor of \(k\). Such a prime exists because \(k>T\ge1\), and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic shows both that \(P\mid k\) and that every prime divisor of \(k\) is at most \(P\).

There are two cases.

1. Suppose \(P\le B\). Then every prime divisor of \(k\) is at most \(B\). Apply the factor-balancing lemma with \(m=k\) and \(N=n\). Its hypotheses follow from \(k\le n\) and (1). We obtain
\[
k=xy,\qquad x,y\le T.
\]
Because \(k>0\), both \(x\) and \(y\) are positive. Moreover, each is at most \(k\): for example, \(y\ge1\) gives \(x\le xy=k\), and similarly for \(y\). Hence \(x,y\le n\). Therefore \(x,y\in\{1,\ldots,\min(T,n)\}\subseteq S_n\), as required.

2. Suppose \(P>B\). Write \(k=Pq\). We claim that \(q\le T\). Otherwise \(q>T\), and then
\[
k=Pq>BT.
\]
But (1) says \(n\le BT\), contradicting \(k\le n\). Thus \(q\le T\). Also \(q\ge1\) and \(q\le k\le n\), so \(q\) belongs to the initial interval in \(S_n\). The number \(P\) is prime and, being a divisor of the positive integer \(k\), satisfies \(P\le k\le n\); hence \(P\in S_n\). Thus \(k=Pq\) is again a product of two members of \(S_n\).

This proves
\[
T_n\subseteq S_n\cdot S_n.
\]
Therefore \(S_n\) is an admissible set in the definition of \(a(n)\), and
\[
a(n)\le |S_n|.
\]
The initial interval contributes at most \(T\) elements, while the prime part contributes exactly \(\pi(n)\) elements. The two parts may overlap, which can only reduce the cardinality of their union. Hence
\[
a(n)\le (\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor+1)^3+\pi(n)
\qquad(n\ge1).
\tag{2}
\]

We next obtain a sufficiently strong elementary lower bound for the prime-counting function. We shall prove that, for all sufficiently large integers \(m\),
\[
m^{3/4}\le \pi(2m).
\tag{3}
\]

Let
\[
C_m=\binom{2m}{m}
\]
be the central binomial coefficient. We need two standard estimates for it.

First, for \(m\ge4\),
\[
4^m<mC_m.
\tag{4}
\]
For completeness, this can be proved by induction. At \(m=4\),
\[
4^4=256<280=4\binom84.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\frac{C_{m+1}}{C_m}
 =\frac{(2m+2)(2m+1)}{(m+1)^2}
 =4-\frac{2}{m+1}.
\]
Thus, if \(4^m<mC_m\), then
\[
4^{m+1}<4mC_m<(4m+2)C_m=(m+1)C_{m+1},
\]
which proves (4).

Second,
\[
C_m\le (2m)^{\pi(2m)}.
\tag{5}
\]
To see this, consider the prime factorization of \(C_m\). Every prime occurring in it is at most \(2m\), since \(C_m\) is formed from factorials involving no integer larger than \(2m\). More precisely, for every prime \(p\), Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_p(C_m)
 =\sum_{j\ge1}
 \left(
 \left\lfloor\frac{2m}{p^j}\right\rfloor
 -2\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^j}\right\rfloor
 \right).
\]
Each summand is either \(0\) or \(1\), because \(\lfloor2x\rfloor-2\lfloor x\rfloor\in\{0,1\}\). A nonzero summand can occur only when \(p^j\le2m\). It follows that
\[
v_p(C_m)\le \lfloor\log_p(2m)\rfloor,
\]
and consequently
\[
p^{v_p(C_m)}\le2m.
\]
Multiplying this bound over the distinct prime divisors of \(C_m\), of which there are at most \(\pi(2m)\), gives (5).

Combining (4) and (5), for every \(m\ge4\) we have
\[
4^m\le m(2m)^{\pi(2m)}.
\tag{6}
\]
We now deduce (3). Suppose, to the contrary, that for arbitrarily large \(m\),
\[
\pi(2m)<m^{3/4}.
\tag{7}
\]
Taking logarithms in (6), and using the nonnegativity of \(\log(2m)\), yields
\[
m\log4
 \le \log m+\pi(2m)\log(2m)
 \le \log m+m^{3/4}\log(2m).
\tag{8}
\]
But
\[
\log m+m^{3/4}\log(2m)=o(m).
\tag{9}
\]
Indeed, \(\log m=o(m)\), and \(\log(2m)=o(m^{1/4})\); multiplying the latter relation by \(m^{3/4}\) gives \(m^{3/4}\log(2m)=o(m)\). Since \(\log4>0\), (9) implies that, for all sufficiently large \(m\),
\[
\log m+m^{3/4}\log(2m)\le \frac{\log4}{2}\,m.
\]
This contradicts (8). Therefore there is an integer \(K\) such that
\[
m^{3/4}\le\pi(2m)\qquad(m\ge K),
\]
which is (3).

We now compare the nonprime part of the covering set with \(\pi(n)\). First, for every \(n\ge1\), if \(r=\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor\), then \(r\ge1\), \(r^4\le n\), and hence \(r\le n^{1/4}\). Also \(r+1\le2r\). Therefore
\[
(\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor+1)^3
 =(r+1)^3
 \le(2r)^3
 =8r^3
 \le8n^{3/4}.
\tag{10}
\]

For \(n\ge2\), put \(m=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Then \(m\ge1\), \(2m\le n\), and the deliberately coarse but convenient inequality \(n\le4m\) holds. From (10), monotonicity of the function \(x\mapsto x^{3/4}\), and \(4^{3/4}\le4\), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor+1)^3
 &\le8n^{3/4}\\
 &\le8(4m)^{3/4}\\
 &\le32m^{3/4}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

Choose
\[
N_0=\max(2K,2).
\]
If \(n\ge N_0\) and \(m=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), then \(m\ge K\). By (3), the monotonicity of \(\pi\), and \(2m\le n\),
\[
m^{3/4}\le\pi(2m)\le\pi(n).
\]
Using this in (11) gives
\[
(\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor+1)^3\le32\pi(n).
\tag{12}
\]
Substitution into (2) now yields, for every \(n\ge N_0\),
\[
a(n)\le32\pi(n)+\pi(n)=33\pi(n).
\tag{13}
\]
Since \(n\ge2\), the denominator \(\pi(n)\) is positive, and therefore
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le33
\qquad(n\ge N_0).
\tag{14}
\]

It remains only to control the finite initial range \(2\le n<N_0\) without needing to inspect its members individually. The whole set \(T_n\) is itself admissible: it contains \(1\), and each \(k\in T_n\) is represented as \(k=k\cdot1\). Thus
\[
a(n)\le n.
\tag{15}
\]
For \(n\ge2\), at least the prime \(2\) is counted, so \(\pi(n)\ge1\). Hence, when \(2\le n<N_0\),
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le a(n)\le n\le N_0.
\tag{16}
\]

Finally set
\[
C=\max(33,N_0).
\]
Equation (14) handles \(n\ge N_0\), while (16) handles \(2\le n<N_0\). Consequently, for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le C.
\]
Thus the ratio \(a(n)/\pi(n)\) is bounded as \(n\to\infty\), as claimed.
